messages.content: I want to design a typed FFI that preserves borrowed-memory safety across reentrant C callbacks, asynchronous cancellation, and callback deregistration. It should support zero-copy borrowed buffers while preventing use-after-free under explicit foreign-code contracts. Callback dispatch overhead also needs to stay within 20% of equivalent unchecked bindings, excluding foreign execution.

That sets two constraints on the design: borrowed buffers must remain usable without copying while their lifetime is valid, and the typed boundary must prevent access after that lifetime ends, subject to the stated contracts with foreign code. The safety argument has to hold through reentrant callbacks, cancellation, and deregistration—not just through a straightforward call and return. Separately, the callback-dispatch portion must meet the 20% overhead limit relative to equivalent unchecked bindings; time spent executing foreign code is outside that comparison.
What does “borrowed-memory safety” mean here if the buffer is zero-copy?

Zero-copy means the interface can give foreign code access to the existing buffer rather than making a separate buffer for it. Borrowed-memory safety means that access must remain confined to a period in which the underlying memory is valid for that use. The typed FFI needs to preserve that constraint even when control flow is complicated. Zero-copy does not, by itself, extend the buffer’s lifetime or make later access safe.
So copying the buffer whenever a callback is involved would miss part of the goal?

Yes. The goal explicitly includes supporting zero-copy borrowed buffers. A design that depends on copying every borrowed buffer to avoid lifetime concerns would not fully meet it. The challenge is to make the borrowing relationship safe without relying on a copy as the general answer.
Why do the foreign-code contracts need to be explicit?

A typed interface can only make a sound promise about foreign behavior if the relevant behavior is stated. For borrowed memory, the contract needs to delimit when foreign code may access it and when any possible access has ended. Otherwise, the interface could appear to guarantee safety while foreign code retains a way to use memory after its lifetime. The goal is safety under explicit foreign-code contracts, not an unconditional guarantee against arbitrary behavior by foreign code.
Does the goal already specify the exact wording of those contracts?

No. It calls for explicit foreign-code contracts but does not prescribe their exact form. What matters to this goal is that the contracts provide enough information to justify when a borrow remains valid, including around callbacks, cancellation, and deregistration. The specific representation of those obligations is a design question, not a fact already settled here.
I’m especially worried about a C callback reentering code that interacts with the same borrowed memory.

That is why reentrancy is named explicitly. A safety argument that assumes callbacks cannot nest or cannot lead back into related FFI operations would be insufficient. While a callback is active, reentrant activity must not make a borrowed buffer appear finished and reusable if an allowed access to it is still possible. Conversely, the typed interface must not permit an access merely because an outer callback was once valid if the applicable borrowing conditions no longer hold.
Does reentrancy necessarily mean multiple threads?

No. Reentrancy concerns control entering again before an earlier invocation has finished; it does not, by itself, assert that multiple threads are involved. The goal also names asynchronous cancellation, which introduces its own timing concerns, but it does not specify a threading model. The FFI’s safety conditions should address the behaviors its foreign-code contracts actually permit.
How should I read the cancellation part without assuming a particular cancellation API?

Read it as a lifetime problem: a cancellation event must not cause borrowed storage to be treated as free for reuse while an access permitted by the foreign-code contract can still occur. Nor can a pending operation be assumed to have finished using the buffer solely because cancellation was requested. The goal does not dictate how cancellation is signaled or completed; it requires the typed FFI to preserve safety across that process.
And deregistering a callback has a similar boundary?

Yes, although deregistration and cancellation are distinct events. Deregistration changes whether a callback may be invoked according to the applicable contract, but safety also depends on what that contract says about invocations already in progress or otherwise still possible. The FFI cannot conclude that borrowed memory is no longer accessible merely from the word “deregistered” without the corresponding foreign-code guarantee.
So I should distinguish ‘no new callback may start’ from ‘all callback activity has finished’?

Conceptually, yes. Those statements are not automatically equivalent. If a foreign-code contract establishes one, the typed FFI should not silently assume it establishes the other. That distinction matters when deciding whether memory reachable through a callback may safely cease to be borrowed.
Could I describe the whole safety requirement as making every possible foreign access fit inside a valid borrow?

That is a useful high-level description, provided “possible” is read relative to the explicit foreign-code contracts. Any access those contracts permit must occur while the relevant borrowed memory is valid. Reentrancy, asynchronous cancellation, and callback deregistration are situations in which it can be difficult to know whether such access is still possible; the typed FFI must not lose that distinction.
Would a type signature alone necessarily settle all of those timing questions?

Not necessarily. Types can express borrowing constraints, but their safety claim has to align with what foreign code promises about access and completion. A signature that treats an operation as finished while the foreign contract still permits an access would not establish the desired safety. The goal specifies a typed FFI and explicit contracts, without prescribing exactly how they are represented together.
I also don’t want the safety checks to swamp callback dispatch. What exactly is the performance comparison?

The stated target is for callback dispatch overhead to remain within 20% of equivalent unchecked bindings, with foreign execution excluded. In ordinary time-based terms, that means comparing the dispatch portions of like-for-like bindings and targeting no more than 1.2 times the unchecked dispatch cost. It is a design requirement, not a reported measurement or a claim that a particular implementation has met it.
Why exclude foreign execution from that number?

Because the specified comparison concerns callback dispatch overhead, not the time foreign code spends doing its own work. Including foreign execution could obscure the difference between a typed dispatch path and an equivalent unchecked one. The requirement keeps the 20% limit focused on the binding’s callback-dispatch cost.
Does that 20% allowance weaken the use-after-free requirement?

No. The safety requirement and the performance target must both be met. The overhead limit is not permission to leave a borrowed-memory access unsafe, and the safety requirement does not erase the stated dispatch-cost constraint. The design challenge is to preserve the needed lifetime guarantees while keeping callback dispatch within that comparison.
Would it be fair to say that cancellation and deregistration are not automatically proof that a borrow has ended?

Yes. Neither event, on its own, proves that foreign code can no longer access the borrowed buffer. Whether access has ended depends on the explicit contract and the state of any activity it permits. Treating the event itself as proof, without that support, could allow use-after-free.
What if foreign code simply ignores its stated contract?

The goal qualifies the prevention of use-after-free as being under explicit foreign-code contracts. The typed FFI’s guarantee therefore rests on foreign code satisfying those contracts. It should not present the contract-dependent guarantee as protection against foreign behavior that the contract forbids.
I’d like one concise way to keep the full scope in mind while designing it.

Design a typed FFI in which zero-copy borrowed buffers remain accessible only while their borrow is valid under explicit foreign-code contracts, even through reentrant C callbacks, asynchronous cancellation, and callback deregistration. At the same time, keep callback dispatch overhead within 20% of equivalent unchecked bindings, excluding foreign execution.

For the typed FFI, I’d like to propose pinned borrow guards and atomic generation-tagged callback slots. Cancellation and deregistration would defer reclamation until reentrant dispatches exit, and the foreign-code contracts would require no retention of borrowed memory. How do these pieces fit together?

They divide the problem into related parts. A pinned borrow guard represents a borrow whose memory must remain valid and stable while permitted foreign access is active. An atomic generation-tagged callback slot provides a way to identify a particular callback registration even when slots change. Deferring reclamation keeps resources needed by active, including reentrant, dispatches from being freed merely because cancellation or deregistration occurs. The no-retention contract limits foreign access so that, once the permitted dispatch activity has ended, foreign code cannot still be holding borrowed memory for later use.
Is pinning by itself enough to prevent use-after-free?

No. Pinning addresses stability of the borrowed memory while it is valid; it does not, by itself, establish how long foreign code may access it. The guard and the reclamation rule need to keep the borrow valid for every access the contract permits. The no-retention requirement matters because the FFI cannot safely end a borrow if foreign code is allowed to keep using its pointer afterward.
So the guard is not just a promise that an address will stay the same?

Right. In this proposal, the guard is part of expressing that the borrowed memory remains protected for the relevant foreign access. Address stability is useful for a zero-copy interface, but a stable address would still be unsafe if the memory’s valid lifetime ended too early. Both properties matter.
What role does the generation tag play if a callback slot already exists?

The tag distinguishes a particular registration associated with a slot from another registration that might occupy that slot at a different time. That distinction is relevant when callbacks and deregistration can overlap: slot identity alone need not tell you whether a dispatch refers to the registration it originally encountered. The proposal calls for atomic generation-tagged slots, but it does not yet specify every rule for reading, changing, or validating them.
Does the atomic slot replace the pinned borrow guard?

No. They address different questions. The slot helps identify and coordinate callback registration state. The guard concerns the validity of borrowed memory exposed through the FFI. A correctly identified callback could still be unsafe if it accesses a borrow after that borrow ends; a valid borrow does not, by itself, resolve which callback registration a dispatch belongs to.
I want deregistration to take effect without freeing something an active callback still needs.

That is the purpose of deferred reclamation in the proposal. Deregistration can affect the registration state, while reclamation of resources needed by dispatch waits until the relevant reentrant dispatches exit. The distinction is between changing whether a registration is available and concluding that no active dispatch still depends on it. The proposal does not equate those moments.
Would cancellation follow the same principle?

Yes. The proposed rule applies to both cancellation and deregistration: neither should trigger reclamation while reentrant dispatches that need the resources remain active. Cancellation must not be treated as proof that foreign access to a borrowed buffer has already stopped. The exact cancellation mechanism is not specified here; the proposed lifetime rule is the important part.
Why say ‘until reentrant dispatches exit’ rather than just ‘until the callback returns’?

Because a callback can lead to further dispatch before the earlier dispatch has completed. If reclamation were based only on an incomplete view of that activity, it could occur while a nested dispatch still depends on the registration or borrowed memory. Referring to reentrant dispatches makes the intended boundary broader than one isolated callback invocation.
Does that mean a deregistration request must wait to return until every dispatch exits?

The proposal specifies deferred reclamation, not a particular return-time behavior for the deregistration operation. It says when resources may be reclaimed relative to reentrant dispatches; it does not settle whether an operation waits for that point or reports before reclamation occurs. Either way, the typed FFI must not expose an invalid borrow during the interval.
I’m trying to understand how strict ‘no retention’ has to be.

It has to rule out foreign use of borrowed memory after the access period on which the FFI’s lifetime guarantee relies. If foreign code could keep a borrowed pointer and use it after the relevant dispatches exit and reclamation proceeds, deferring reclamation only until those exits would not prevent use-after-free. The contract therefore needs to make that later use impermissible; merely avoiding a copy does not impose the restriction on foreign code.
Would the no-retention contract alone make the generation tag unnecessary?

Not for the role the proposal assigns it. No retention constrains what foreign code may do with borrowed memory after its permitted access period. A generation tag concerns the identity of a callback registration as slot state changes. Those are separate concerns, even though both contribute to reasoning about a safe callback boundary.
And an atomic generation tag doesn’t mean reclamation can happen immediately?

Correct. Identifying a registration does not make resources used by an active dispatch safe to reclaim. The proposal explicitly defers reclamation after cancellation or deregistration until reentrant dispatches exit. The slot and tag help with registration state; they do not replace that lifetime condition.
How would you describe the zero-copy aspect without implying foreign code owns the buffer?

The foreign code may access the existing borrowed buffer without a copied substitute, under the guard and the explicit no-retention contract. Access to that memory is temporary and contract-bound; zero-copy does not transfer ownership or grant permission to keep a pointer for later use. The proposal aims to preserve the original buffer’s validity throughout permitted access, rather than avoiding the question by copying it.
What if a cancellation arrives while a callback has reentered and another dispatch is active?

Under the proposed rule, cancellation does not reclaim resources still needed by those dispatches. Reclamation is deferred until the reentrant dispatches exit. That is precisely the kind of overlap the proposal is meant to handle; it does not require assuming that cancellation waits for a simple, nonreentrant call-and-return sequence.
What if deregistration and cancellation both concern the same active registration?

The same stated constraint still applies: neither event may cause reclamation before the relevant reentrant dispatches have exited. The proposal identifies atomic generation-tagged slots for registration state and deferred reclamation for active dispatches, but it does not specify a precedence rule or a detailed state transition for simultaneous events. Those details would need to preserve the stated lifetime condition.
Could the pinned guard be released as soon as deregistration is requested?

Not if an active dispatch can still access the borrowed memory under the foreign-code contract. A request to deregister does not itself establish that all permitted access has ended. The guard must continue to protect the borrow for the necessary period, and reclamation must respect the active reentrant dispatches. Once that activity has exited, the no-retention contract is what rules out later foreign use of the borrow.
Is the proposal claiming that any C API can satisfy the no-retention requirement?

No. It explicitly requires a no-retention contract. If a foreign API permits retaining and later using borrowed pointers beyond the protected period, this proposal’s stated condition would not cover that behavior. Whether a particular C API offers the needed contract is not established by the proposal itself.
Does ‘atomic’ settle all of the concurrency and reentrancy details?

No. ‘Atomic generation-tagged callback slots’ names a proposed mechanism, but it does not specify a complete synchronization argument. In particular, the proposal does not state how dispatch establishes its claim on resources before they can be reclaimed. Any detailed implementation would need to make the slot operations and deferred-reclamation boundary work together; merely calling a slot atomic would not prove borrowed-memory safety.
How should we treat the 20% callback-dispatch overhead target while considering this proposal?

It remains a requirement to evaluate, not an achieved result. The relevant comparison is callback dispatch against equivalent unchecked bindings, with foreign execution excluded, and the overhead must stay within 20%. Pinned guards, atomic generation-tagged slots, and deferred reclamation may have dispatch costs; the proposal does not provide measurements establishing that they meet the limit.
So we need both the lifetime argument and the dispatch-cost comparison, without assuming either is already proved?

Exactly. The proposal describes how to approach the safety problem: protect zero-copy borrows with pinned guards, distinguish registrations with atomic generation-tagged slots, defer cancellation and deregistration reclamation until reentrant dispatches exit, and require foreign code not to retain borrowed memory. It does not itself establish that every implementation of those ideas prevents use-after-free or keeps dispatch overhead within 20% of equivalent unchecked bindings, excluding foreign execution.
Does the C API guarantee that a deregistration acknowledgment excludes callbacks queued on other threads but not yet entered?

That guarantee is not established by what we know here. The key question is whether the acknowledgment means only that deregistration has been accepted, or whether it also guarantees that a callback already queued on another thread cannot subsequently begin. Those are different guarantees, and the C API’s contract would need to say which one it provides.
If the callback is already queued, why wouldn’t acknowledgment cover it?

Because a queued callback has not necessarily entered its dispatch yet. An API could stop future scheduling while leaving previously queued work able to start; another API could guarantee that acknowledgment accounts for such work. We cannot infer either behavior merely from the word “acknowledgment.”
I’m asking about callbacks queued on other threads specifically, not callbacks already running when deregistration happens.

Right. An already-running callback is visibly in progress. Your question concerns a narrower and less obvious interval: a callback has been queued on another thread, has not entered yet, and might begin after acknowledgment. The contract must explicitly resolve whether acknowledgment rules out that later entry.
Would a guarantee that ‘no callbacks are currently executing’ answer it?

Not by itself. A callback that is queued but not yet entered is not currently executing. To answer your question, the guarantee must also address whether such a callback may enter after acknowledgment.
What if the API says ‘no new callbacks will be scheduled after deregistration’?

That still leaves open what happens to callbacks scheduled or queued before deregistration. Your question is about that already-queued work, so a prohibition on new scheduling alone does not establish that acknowledgment excludes it.
So ‘no new scheduling’ and ‘no later entry’ should not be treated as interchangeable?

Exactly. The former concerns when work is queued; the latter concerns when callback execution may begin. A queue can separate those moments, especially across threads. The acknowledgment’s meaning needs to be clear about the second moment to resolve this question.
Could I assume that acknowledging deregistration drains the other threads’ queues?

No such queue-draining guarantee has been stated. It would be one possible way for an API to exclude queued callbacks, but the question is whether this C API actually guarantees the outcome. We should not infer queue draining, or any other mechanism, from acknowledgment alone.
Does the wording need to mention queues explicitly?

Not necessarily. What matters is an unambiguous guarantee about behavior: after acknowledgment, can any callback for that registration begin, including one queued earlier on another thread? Wording that clearly answers that may suffice without describing how the API handles its queues.
Suppose the acknowledgment excludes callbacks queued on other threads but not yet entered. What would that let us conclude?

On that stated assumption, those queued callbacks cannot subsequently enter for that registration after acknowledgment. That would resolve the particular uncertainty you identified. It would not, by itself, say that callbacks which entered before acknowledgment have finished; that is a separate question.
And if the acknowledgment does not exclude them?

Then a callback queued before deregistration could still enter afterward, if the API’s contract permits that behavior. The typed FFI could not treat acknowledgment alone as proof that no later callback entry is possible. That is a conditional implication, not a claim that this C API behaves that way.
Why does ‘not yet entered’ matter so much for the borrowed buffer?

Because a callback that enters later may attempt an access that the FFI needs to keep safe. If the interface ends a borrow on the assumption that acknowledgment prevents further entry, but the C API permits a previously queued callback to enter afterward, that assumption would be unsound. Whether that situation is possible depends on the API’s guarantee.
Can the fact that deregistration was acknowledged serve as a lifetime boundary without more detail?

Not for this particular concern. To use acknowledgment as evidence that callbacks queued on other threads cannot begin later, the contract must actually give it that meaning. Otherwise, acknowledgment leaves the status of those not-yet-entered callbacks unresolved.
Is this asking whether callbacks are queued, or what happens if they are?

It asks what the acknowledgment guarantees about callbacks that are queued on other threads but have not yet entered. It does not assert that any such callbacks exist in a particular run. The important case is whether, if one is queued, acknowledgment excludes its later entry.
Can we answer yes or no from the proposal for generation-tagged callback slots?

No. A proposed mechanism for managing callback slots does not establish what the foreign C API promises when it acknowledges deregistration. The yes-or-no answer has to come from that API’s contract, not from the FFI proposal.
Then what exact distinction should I look for in the C API’s contract?

Look for whether acknowledgment merely stops new registrations or scheduling, whether it accounts for callbacks already executing, and—most specifically here—whether it prevents callbacks already queued on other threads from entering afterward. Only the last point directly answers your question about queued, not-yet-entered callbacks.
My hypothesis is that the C API’s deregistration acknowledgment acts as a queue-drain barrier: under concurrent dispatch, zero queued callbacks enter after the acknowledgment returns.

That is a precise hypothesis about the acknowledgment’s effect. It says that even if callback work is queued while dispatch is happening concurrently, none of those queued callbacks can begin callback execution after deregistration acknowledgment returns. It remains a hypothesis, not an established guarantee of the C API.
Does “queue-drain barrier” mean the API must literally empty a queue?

Not necessarily. Here it describes the observable guarantee you are proposing: zero queued callbacks enter after acknowledgment returns. The API might achieve that outcome in different ways. The hypothesis does not specify an internal queue implementation or how the barrier works.
I want to be clear about the timing. Is the boundary when deregistration is requested or when its acknowledgment returns?

The hypothesis places the boundary at the return of the deregistration acknowledgment. It does not say that queued callbacks are excluded from entering as soon as deregistration is requested, or at some earlier point while acknowledgment is pending.
What about a callback queued on another thread that starts just before acknowledgment returns?

The hypothesis does not exclude that entry: it says zero queued callbacks enter *after* the acknowledgment returns. A callback that enters before that return is outside this particular prohibition, even if its execution continues afterward.
So the hypothesis doesn’t imply all callbacks have finished executing when acknowledgment returns?

Correct. Entry and completion are different events. A callback may have entered before the acknowledgment returns and still be executing afterward without contradicting the proposed queue-drain barrier. The hypothesis addresses later entry by queued callbacks, not the completion of callbacks already entered.
Why include ‘under concurrent dispatch’ rather than imagining everything is sequential?

It makes the scope explicit: the proposed guarantee is meant to hold even when callback dispatch overlaps deregistration. The interesting case is precisely when another thread may have callback work queued or be about to enter a callback while acknowledgment is in progress. A sequential example alone would not express that concurrent boundary.
Does the hypothesis specifically address callbacks queued on other threads but not yet entered?

Yes. If such a callback is still queued and has not entered when acknowledgment returns, the hypothesized barrier says it will not enter afterward. That is the aspect of acknowledgment needed to answer the question about queued work on other threads—provided the hypothesis turns out to match the C API’s actual contract.
Could acknowledgment simply mean ‘we won’t queue anything new’ and still satisfy this hypothesis?

Not if an already-queued callback could enter after acknowledgment returns. Stopping new queuing addresses work created later; the queue-drain-barrier hypothesis also excludes later entry by work that was already queued. The two statements should not be treated as equivalent.
If no queued callback enters after the return, can I also say no callback enters after the return?

That broader wording needs care. The hypothesis explicitly concerns *queued callbacks*. It does not separately define every possible route by which a callback might enter, so it is safest to retain its stated scope rather than silently broaden it to all possible callback entries.
Would a callback already inside the dispatch path but not yet inside the callback count as ‘entered’?

The hypothesis depends on a clear meaning of callback entry, but it does not supply a finer-grained dispatch model. For the proposed guarantee to be useful, “enter” should refer consistently to the point at which callback execution begins. Whether a particular in-between state is classified as queued or already entered would have to be clear in the C API’s contract; we should not invent that classification here.
How does this hypothesis relate to the zero-copy borrowed buffer concern?

If the hypothesis holds, acknowledgement’s return would rule out a queued callback entering later and unexpectedly accessing a borrowed buffer. That would resolve one possible source of post-acknowledgment access. It would not alone settle the lifetime of a callback that entered before the return and remains active, or eliminate the need for the stated no-retention contract.
Would it make deferred reclamation until reentrant dispatches exit unnecessary?

The hypothesis alone would not justify that conclusion. Excluding later entry by queued callbacks is different from showing that dispatches which already entered have exited. The proposed reclamation condition concerns active reentrant dispatches, while this hypothesis concerns queued callbacks entering after acknowledgment returns.
Could a running callback reenter after the acknowledgment returns without contradicting the hypothesis?

That question cannot be fully resolved from this hypothesis alone. It excludes entry by queued callbacks after acknowledgment returns, including under concurrent dispatch; it does not spell out how the C API treats new entry arising from an already-running callback. We should not assume that the phrase ‘queue-drain barrier’ settles every form of reentrancy.
And cancellation isn’t covered by this acknowledgment hypothesis, right?

Right. This hypothesis is specifically about the C API’s *deregistration acknowledgment* and queued callbacks under concurrent dispatch. It does not state an analogous guarantee for asynchronous cancellation.
What evidence would distinguish this from the weaker ‘no newly queued callbacks’ interpretation?

The decisive point would be whether the C API guarantees the outcome for callback work queued before acknowledgment returns but not yet entered: can it enter afterward? An explicit contract saying it cannot would support the queue-drain-barrier interpretation; wording that addresses only new scheduling would leave this specific hypothesis unestablished. No such evidence is supplied here.
So until that is checked, how should I phrase it?

Phrase it conditionally: “Hypothesis: the C API’s deregistration acknowledgment is a queue-drain barrier; under concurrent dispatch, zero queued callbacks enter after it returns.” That preserves the proposed timing and scope without presenting the guarantee as verified.
Let’s run QueueDrainRace across 100,000 queued-dispatch/deregistration races. It should compare callback-entry timestamps against the deregistration acknowledgment under ThreadSanitizer.

That activity targets the queue-drain-barrier hypothesis directly. Across 100,000 races between queued dispatch and deregistration, QueueDrainRace would compare when callbacks enter with when acknowledgment returns. The outcome of interest is whether any queued callback enters after that return, including when dispatch and deregistration overlap. Running under ThreadSanitizer adds race-detection scrutiny, but no observations or results have been reported yet.
Why compare callback-entry timestamps rather than just record whether a callback happened?

Because the hypothesis turns on a specific ordering, not on the mere presence of a callback. A queued callback that enters before acknowledgment returns is not the same case as one that enters afterward. Comparing entry timestamps against acknowledgment is intended to distinguish those cases.
Is the acknowledgment boundary its start or its return?

Its return. The hypothesis says zero queued callbacks enter after the deregistration acknowledgment returns under concurrent dispatch. An entry while acknowledgment is still pending would not, by itself, contradict that wording.
What does one of the 100,000 races need to put in contention?

The activity specifies a queued-dispatch/deregistration race: queued callback dispatch and deregistration must overlap in a way that makes their ordering relevant. It does not prescribe a particular scheduler, queue implementation, or test harness. The comparison that matters remains callback entry relative to acknowledgment.
Does QueueDrainRace measure when a callback finishes?

The stated activity measures callback-entry timing against acknowledgment. It does not call for comparing callback completion times. That matches the particular hypothesis, which concerns whether queued callbacks *enter* after acknowledgment returns, rather than whether callbacks that entered earlier have finished.
Suppose an entry timestamp falls after acknowledgment. What would that mean for this activity?

If it is an entry by a queued callback and the ordering is accurately established, it would be the kind of observation that conflicts with the proposed zero-after-acknowledgment condition. That is a conditional interpretation of a possible observation, not a claim that QueueDrainRace has observed one.
And if every recorded entry is before acknowledgment in all 100,000 races, does that prove the C API contract?

No. It would describe what those 100,000 races observed, but a finite set of executions cannot by itself establish a universal C API guarantee. The activity can probe the hypothesis under concurrent dispatch; it should not be described as having proved the contract merely because a particular outcome might recur in the test.
Why specify 100,000 rather than say ‘run it many times’?

Because 100,000 is the stated scope of the activity. It makes the planned number of queued-dispatch/deregistration races concrete. It does not imply that those races will cover every possible interleaving or that any result is already known.
Where does ThreadSanitizer fit into the comparison?

QueueDrainRace is to run under ThreadSanitizer while comparing callback-entry timestamps with acknowledgment. ThreadSanitizer may expose data races during those concurrent executions. Its involvement does not replace the ordering comparison: a data-race report and a queued callback entering after acknowledgment would be different observations.
Would a clean ThreadSanitizer run establish the queue-drain barrier?

No. The absence of a ThreadSanitizer report in a run would not, on its own, show that zero queued callbacks can enter after acknowledgment returns. The queue-drain claim is about callback-entry ordering, so the planned timestamp comparison remains necessary; neither observation alone turns a finite test into a universal guarantee.
Could a ThreadSanitizer warning alone show that a callback entered after acknowledgment?

Not necessarily. A warning would concern a detected data race, while the hypothesis concerns the order of callback entry and acknowledgment. You would still need the relevant entry-versus-acknowledgment ordering to address that hypothesis. The activity includes both the comparison and execution under ThreadSanitizer without treating them as interchangeable.
I want to avoid counting a callback that was already active when acknowledgment returned as a violation.

That distinction follows from comparing *entry* times. If a callback entered before acknowledgment returned, its continuing execution afterward would not be a post-acknowledgment entry. QueueDrainRace’s stated comparison is aimed at the time it enters, not the time it exits.
What about a callback that was queued before acknowledgment but enters afterward?

That is the central case. Under the queue-drain-barrier hypothesis, zero such queued callbacks enter after acknowledgment returns, even with concurrent dispatch. QueueDrainRace is planned to look for the ordering that would distinguish that case from a callback that entered before the boundary.
Does the plan say how the timestamps will be captured or synchronized?

No. It specifies QueueDrainRace, 100,000 queued-dispatch/deregistration races, the comparison between callback-entry timestamps and acknowledgment, and execution under ThreadSanitizer. It does not specify timestamp instrumentation or synchronization details. Those details would matter when interpreting an apparent ordering, but they are not established here.
Is this also a performance test for the 20% callback-dispatch overhead limit?

No performance comparison is specified for QueueDrainRace. This activity evaluates the proposed queue-drain behavior through entry timing under concurrent dispatch and ThreadSanitizer. It does not measure callback dispatch overhead against equivalent unchecked bindings or establish whether the 20% limit is met.
Then the activity is about a narrow deregistration question, not every FFI lifetime condition?

Yes. It probes whether queued callbacks enter after deregistration acknowledgment returns under concurrent dispatch. That ordering matters to borrowed-memory safety, but QueueDrainRace as stated does not evaluate every condition involving pinned borrow guards, cancellation, active reentrant dispatches, or foreign-code no-retention contracts.
How should I state the activity without sounding as though it has already been run?

“Run QueueDrainRace across 100,000 queued-dispatch/deregistration races, comparing callback-entry timestamps against the deregistration acknowledgment under ThreadSanitizer.” That states the planned activity and its comparison without asserting a result.
QueueDrainRace has run. It recorded 23 callback entries after deregistration acknowledgment in 100,000 races, and ThreadSanitizer reported no data races.

The recorded result is 23 callback entries after deregistration acknowledgment across the 100,000 QueueDrainRace races. Separately, ThreadSanitizer reported no data races during the run. Those are two different observations: one concerns the timing of callback entry, and the other concerns data-race reports.
When I report the 23, should I describe them as callbacks that finished after acknowledgment?
No. The recorded events are callback *entries* after acknowledgment. The result does not say when those callbacks finished.
And the acknowledgment is the reference point for each recorded entry?
Yes. The reported ordering places those 23 callback entries after the corresponding deregistration acknowledgment. The result is about that relative timing in the QueueDrainRace runs.
Does “23 in 100,000 races” tell us how many separate threads produced the entries?
No. It gives the number of post-acknowledgment callback entries and the number of races, but it does not report how those entries were distributed among threads or individual races.
How should I read the clean ThreadSanitizer report alongside those timestamps?

Keep the findings separate. ThreadSanitizer reported no data races; QueueDrainRace nevertheless recorded the stated callback-entry timing. A lack of reported data races does not erase or reinterpret the timing observations.
Does the ThreadSanitizer result mean every interaction in the run was safe?

That conclusion is not supplied by the result. What is reported is specifically that ThreadSanitizer found no data races. It is not a general finding about every safety property of the FFI or the C API.
Can I infer the precise sequence inside deregistration from the 23 entries?

Not from this report alone. It states when those callback entries occurred relative to acknowledgment, but it does not describe the internal steps of deregistration or how callback work was handled before entry.
What is the most exact way to state the evidence without adding an interpretation?
“QueueDrainRace recorded 23 callback entries after deregistration acknowledgment in 100,000 races; ThreadSanitizer reported no data races.”

Here is a revised hypothesis about deregistration: its acknowledgment blocks new enqueue admissions but permits callbacks that were queued beforehand to enter. If that is the contract, safe reclamation requires explicit queue quiescence.

That separates two events that an acknowledgment need not combine. Under the hypothesis, no new callback work is admitted to the queue after acknowledgment, but work admitted before it can still enter a callback afterward. It limits foreign code’s ability to keep borrowed access beyond the period the FFI protects. A zero-copy binding may expose existing memory during a valid borrow, but it cannot safely end that borrow if foreign code is permitted to retain a pointer and use it later. The manifest’s no-retention guarantee supplies the contract needed to rule out that later use.

No. Silence does not establish the no-retention guarantee needed for safe borrowed access. Under this proposal, the binding should reject borrowing that cannot be justified by the audited manifest, rather than treating an unspecified foreign behavior as safe.

Reentrant callbacks can make borrowed access overlap with another entry into the binding before an earlier dispatch has finished. No. This is a proposal about compiling contract-indexed bindings and what borrowing they permit.
